ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Non-availability of Urea 
*641. SHRI  DIPANKAR  MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-itme 
titled, "more fertilizer units should be closed", appearing in the Statesman 
dated 14th April, 2002; 
(b) if so, whether Government are taking into consideration the 
absence of any Urea producing units in West Bengal and Bihar, after the 
proposed closure of Haldia, Durgapur, Barauni and Jharkhand; 
(c) if so, the impact of non-availability of Urea in those States, after 
the proposed removal of administrative pricing system of Urea and ECA; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to have green-field or brown-field 
Urea producing units in these States? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. A Group of Ministers (G.M) has been constituted in June, 
2001 to examine the comprehensive rehabilitation/ restructuring proposals of 
the four sick fertilizer Public Sector  Undertakings (PSUs) of Hindustan 
Fertilizer Corporation Ltd. (HFC), 
1 
 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
Fertilizer Corporation of India Ltd. (FCI), Projects & Development India Ltd. 
(PDIL) and Pyrites, Phosphates & Chemicals Ltd. (PPCL), based on their 
unit-wise techno-economic viability. GM's recommendations are to be 
submitted to the competent authority in the Government. 
(c) There is no proposal at pres ent for immediate removal of 
distribution control on Urea. 
(d) There is no decision on any fresh investment for a new unit under 
public/cooperative sector. Setting up of fertilizer plants in the private sector is 
not subject to any licensing requirements.

SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL: Si r, this problem of ticketless travel in the 
railways is a very big problem, and th e Railways are really seized of the 
matter also. In fact, it is an on-going pr ocess to have a regular check, and we 
have various systems by which these 
12 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
checkings are being done. Apart from the Travelling Ticket Examiners being 
posted, we have also made special efforts to tackle this menace. For example, 
we have a fortress check, wherein the tr ain. or, the station is encircled from 
all sides, by mobilsing a large number of ticket checking staff. Then, we also 
organise ambush checks, where the trai n is stopped at a pre-planned place, 
during the run-of the train, where checks are conducted by the ticket 
checking staff, so as to have an el ement of surprise. Then, we have the 
replacement checks, within divisions, where the staff stationed at one place 
conducts check at other places, so as to eliminate local influences. Then there 
are inter-Railway and inter-Divisional checks. Then there are concentrated 
spot, checks at entry and exist gates and at other locations at stations, 
continuously, for a number of days at important stations. We are also 
organising mobile checks conducted by the ticket checking staff, in groups, 
in various trains. Magesterial checks are also organised wherein Magistrate 
with the help of the Railway Police conducts the checks. 
Even during this year, we organised massive railway ticket checking. 
The first of it was mentioned by the hon. Member, which forms part of the 
substance of this question. From 21st and 27th, during the month of January, 
organised checks were conducted in three important stations at Delhi, New 
Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddhin railway stations. About 3,384 persons were 
apprehended and an amount of Rs. 3.97 lakhs collected. During the month of 
February, a massive check was organised all over India. About 8,756 persons 
were apprehended. From 16th April to 30th April, a massive operation was 
organised, called Jagru, in which many important persons and people 
belonging to various political parties and Government officials were 
apprehended. These are all on-going effo rts to see that ticketless travelling is 
effectively countered. Of course, this  will require cooperation of the public. 
We are organising a public education programme. It is also being ensured 
that the people who come to the station at the last minute are provided tickets 
without any difficulty. Separate counters are being opened for the purpose. 
We are thinking of providing facilities of issuing tickets, or, platform tickets 
in important cities for those people who come to the station at the last 
moment and want these tickets. This is a comprehensive scheme,by which, 
this menance could be countered.

Fish landing centre in Karnataka 
*652. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government had accorded approval for construction of a 
fish landing centre at Kodibengre in Karnataka; 
(b) if so, what are the details in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the Karnataka Government has intimated the 
revised estimated cost of construction of the fish landing centre and has 
requested for releasing the 1 st instalment of the revised cost; and 
(d) if so, what are the details in this regard and the reaction of 
Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. The Government of India had accorded the approval to the proposal of 
the Government of Karnataka for construction of fish landing centre at 
Kodibengre at a total cost of Rs. 55.50 lakhs in March, 1993 under the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme on fishing harbour facilities at major and minor 
ports with 50% grant assistance. The first instalment of central share 
amounting to Rs. 8.00 lakhs was released in March 1993 and second 
Instalment of Rs. 19.75 lakhs in March 1995. This entire central share of Rs. 
27.75 lakhs was released to the Stat e Government for completion of the 
project by 1995 itself. The terms and conditions under which the project 
approved are at Statement -I (See below) and details of the items and their 
cost approved by Government of India are at Statement-ll. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Governme nt of Karnataka first submitted a 
Revised Cost Estimate (RCE) proposal with cost escalation from Rs. 55.50 
lakhs to Rs. 111.00 lakhs in August, 1998 and again second RCE proposal for 
Rs. 191.00 lakhs in July, 2001. 
The main reasons attributed by the Government of Karnataka for time 
and cost over run are; (i) Non-availability of Government land for 
development of the fish landing centre, due to which an area 
46 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
100m x 50m is proposed for reclamation, (ii) changes in design of foundation 
of auction hall, (iii) addition of new items of work. 
The justifications furnished for time and cost overrun are not 
acceptable by the Union Government. Th e State Government has also not 
consulted the Central Government for approval of the deviation proposed in 
the original plan of construction. As per the terms and conditions of 
sanctioning of the project vide item No. (iii) of Annexure-I, any escalation in 
the cost of the project is to be borne by the State Government. Further, as per 
the approved provisions of the Centra lly Sponsored Scheme, cost escalation 
in a project will be permitted only under two circumstances viz. (i) time 
overrun on account of natural calamities such as cyclone etc. (ii) disputes over 
contractual works in a court of Law. 
Under these circumstances the RCE proposal of Government of 
Karnataka has not been considered for approval by the Government of India.

NIMS as Institution of excellence 
*653.SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
published in the Deccan Chronicle date d 11th April, 2002 under the caption, 
"NIMS in the good books of UGC Panel: Committee Chief pats institute for 
research work, low cost of medicine"; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether it is proposed to formally declare the Nizam's Institute of 
Medical Sciences (NIMS) as an Institution of Excellence, under section 12B 
of the UGC Act, 1956; and 
(d) if so, when and if not, the reasons therefor/ 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (S HRIMATI) RITA VERMA]. (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) According to the information furnished by the University 
Grants Commission, no proposal from Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences 
is under consideration of UGC for declaring it as an Institution of Excellence. 
Section 12B of the UGC Act lays down that a University can receive grant 
from the Central Government or the Commission or any other organization 
receiving any funds from the Central Gove rnment only after it is declared to 
be fit by UGC for receiving such  grants. The NIMS has accordingly 
submitted a proposal to the UGC to declare it fit to receive Central grant 
under the said Section of the Act. In this context, the UGC has constituted a 
Committee as referred to under part (a) of the question. The Scheme for 
identifying institution as "Univers ities with Potential for Excellence" is 
different one for which there is a separate procedure laid down by the UGC.

*654. SHRI SURESH PACHOU RI: Will the Minister of

(a) what has been the increas e in procurement prices vis-a-vis issue 
prices of wheat and rice during 1991 -92 to 1996-97 and 1997-98 to 2001-
2002; 
(b) how far the cost of production of wheat and rice moved during the 
above period; and 
(c) whether the farmers have not been  compensated for the increase in 
the cost of production of wheat and rice during the last five years? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) The 
Minimum Support Price (MSP) of paddy was increased from Rs. 230 per 
quintal in 1991 -92 to Rs. 380 in 1996-97 showing an increase of 65.2%. 
Similarly, the MSP of paddy (common), fixed at Rs. 415 per quintal in 1997-
98, was raised to Rs. 530 per quintal in 2001 -02 showing an increase of 
27.7%. 
The MSP of wheat was raised from Rs. 275 per quintal in 1991-92 to 
Rs. 475 (inclusive of the bonus of Rs. 60 per quintal) in 1996-97 showing an 
increase of 72.7%. Similarly, the MSP of wheat was raised from Rs. 510 per 
quintal in 1997-98 (inclusive of the bonus of Rs. 55 per. quintal), to Rs. 620 
per quintal in 2001-02, showing an increase of 21.6%. 
The Targeted Public Disribution Sy stem (TPDS) replaced the PDS in 
June 1997. The TPDS System follows a two-tier subsidised pricing structure 
for Families Below Poverty Line (BPL ) and for those Above Poverty Line 
(APL). It is, therefor, difficult to meas ure the increase in the CIP of rice and 
wheat over this period. However, a Stat ement showing central issue prices of 
wheat and rice during 1990-91 to 2000-01 is enclosed (Statement-I). 
(b) As per the latest information available, a statement showing cost of 
production of wheat, and paddy in major growing States between 1991 -92 to 
1998-99 is also enclosed (Statement-ll).

4677. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have launched a new scheme to make water 
more accessible to farmers; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme; 
(c) whether Andhra Pradesh has also been included under the project; 
and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. In order to exploit the ground water potential available in eastern 
region. Government of India has approved a new Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of "On Farm Water Management" which has been launched during 
the year 2001-2002 for increasing crop production in Eastern India. Under the 
scheme financial assistance for.sinking Shallow Tube Wells/Low Lift 
Irrigation points, electric/diesel water pumping sets and dug wells (for plateau 
regions only) will be provided to th e farmers through NABARD as credit 
linked scheme. The funding pattern of the scheme will be on 20:30:50 basis 
i.e., 20% as contribution fr om the beneficiaries, 30% as Government of India 
assistance as subsidy and remaining 50% as loan from the 
86

commercial/State cooperative/rural banks. This scheme is to be implemented 
in ten states viz. Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, 
Manipur, Mizoram, Orissa, Eastern UP and West Bengal. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. The Scheme is approved only for Eastern India.

agricultural graduates from Andhra Pradesh have responded for undergoing

4679. DR. DASARI  NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of

(a) whether fishing harbour facilities are being provided at all the major 
and minor ports of the country to boost fishery industry in the country;

(c) whether Government propose to make it compulsory for every port 
to have fishing harbours; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NA RAYAN YADAV): (a) No, Sir. 
Fishing Harbours are developed at Major and Minor Ports on a need based 
manner. 
(b) In order to augment marine fish production, a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme on "Fishing Harbour Facilities at Major & Minor Ports" is being 
implemented with the objective of providing infrastructure facilities for safe 
landing and berthing of traditional fishing craft and motorised and 
mechanised fishing vessels. Since inception of the scheme six major fishing 
harbours each one at Major Ports of Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Cochin, 
Calcutta (Roychowk), Paradip and Mumbai have been developed. Port-wise 
details of these Major Fishing Harbours is enclosed {See below). Besides, 50 
minor fishing harbours and 171 fish landing centres have also been

Expenses on cultivation in fixing MSP 
† 4681. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any representation from 
farmers in the country, demanding to pay special attention to the expenses 
incurred by them on cultivation, while deciding the Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) of their produces; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any action thereon, so far; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) 
Representations about the fixation of Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) are 
received from farmers and due note is taken thereof. The cost of production is 
the most important factor taken into account by the CACP while formulating 
its recommendations on price policy of agricultural commodities. The cost of 
production covers not only paid out costs but also imputed value of owned 
assets including land and family labour for which the farmers do not incur 
cash expenses. The Government, while fixing MSPs, duly takes into account 
the recommendations of the CACP, views of State Governments and 
concerned Central Ministries alongwith other factors considered important in 
price fixation.

4682.   DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
SHRI GHULAM NABIAZAD: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India's agricultural production for 2001-2002 is set to grow 
7.2 per cent;

92 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, whether the foodgrain production was expected to 
grow by 7.6 per cent while non-foodgrain production would increase 
by 6.6 per cent;

production has been handsome, but it reflected decline in the last 
two years; 
(d) whether India's foodgrain stocks were expected to reach 75 millon 
tonnes by July, 2002; and 
(e) if so, efforts are being made to improve the output of agricultural 
growth in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) 
According to the index of agricultural production with base triennium ending 
1981-82=100, the growth rate of production of foodgrains. non-foodgrains 
and all principal crops during 2001-2002 is expected to be 8.57%, 5.03% and 
7.10% respectively as per the advance estimates on 5.4.2002. 
During 1999-2000, while the foodgrains production had registered a 
positive growth, that of non-foodgrain and all principal crops had shown a 
decline. During 2000-01, all three groups viz. foodgrains, non-foodgrains and 
all principal crops had registered a decline. 
(d) The stock of foodgrains in the Central pool as on 1.7.2002 is likely 
to be 62.00 million tonnes. 
(e) The agricultural production in the country shows a long-term 
upward trend. In order to further improve the performance of the agriculture 
sector, the Government have launched various new initiatives such as 
promotion of watershed development programmes, 
93

emphasis on developing and promoting new technologies, measures for 
increasing availability of agricultural credit, Market Information Network and 
National Agriculture Insurance Scheme etc. Besides, the Government also 
encourage farmers to increase production through price policy which includes 
implementation of Minimum Support Price and Market Intervention 
Schemes, procurement by public agencies and by using instruments of trade. 
Apart from these, the Government have also switched over from the 
conventional schematic approach to macro-management from November, 
2000 for providing assistance to the States. The Macro-Management Scheme 
integrates 27 schemes into one for supplementing and complementing the 
efforts of State Governments through work plans. This gives flexibility to 
States to address specific problems faced by them depending on local 
requirements, avoid overlapping in the contents of different schemes and aim 
at all-round development of agriculture.

Risk Analysis Report by APEDA 
4689. SHRI HARENDRA SINGH MALIK: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Agricultural and Processed Food Export Development 
Authority (APEDA) has submitted a risk analysis report to the 
Department of Agriculture (DOA), but no action has yet been taken 
thereon; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to implement the report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (c) 
No, Sir. No Pest Risk Analysis (PRA) study has been submitted by 
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority 
(APEDA) to the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation (DAC). 
However, APEDA has submitted a list of pests on apples occurring in China. 
On the basis of available information, including the status and 
distribution of endemic pests and the list provided by APEDA, PRA study on 
apples has been completed by the Direct orate of Plant Protection, Quarantine 
& Storage, DAC. As a result of PRA study, the potential pest of Plant 
Quarantine significance have been identified for imposing import restrictions 
by specifying additional declarations and special conditions on Phytosanitary 
Certificate (PSC) to be issued by the country of origin. 
All the imported plants, plant material including fruits are subjected to 
thorough Plant quarantine screening, inspection, laboratory tests and 
treatment before their release at the por t of entry so as to ensure that no 
exotic pest/insect enter the country and cause any harm to Indian fruits 
including apples.

SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that private sector fertilizer producing 
factories had received additional subsidy from Government, during 
the last three years; 
(b) if so, which are those factories and the amount of additional 
subsidies received by them during that period, year-wise; and 
(c) whether this additional subsidy has been recovered by 
Government; if not, the outstanding amount yet to be recovered, upto March, 
2002? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (c) 
Urea, being the only fertilizer at present under statutory 
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
116 

[1.0 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
price, distribution and movement control, is covered under Retention Price 
Scheme (RPS); and urea manufacturers are paid subsidy as the difference 
between the retention price and the statutorily notified sale price. Under RPS, 
the retention prices (cost of production plus 12% post tax return) are fixed 
unit-wise having regard to a combination of norms and actuals of various cost 
elements. Operational cost of production of urea units differs not only from 
unit to unit but also from month to month, depending upon, inter-alia, the 
health and vintage of the plant, the f eedstock used, the levels of capacity 
utilization, specific consumption and inputs cost. Such computation is not 
related to the unit being in private or in cooperative/ public sector. 
The Government is seized of the matter relating to excess arawal of 
subsidy by some urea manufacturing companies, whether in public, private or 
cooperative sector on account of understatement of capacity of their units. The 
Government had appointed a Committee of Experts under the chairmanship of 
Dr. Y.K. Alagh to address the total issue of the assessment of capacity 
including recoveries that may have to be effected. The Committee has 
submitted its report on 29.3.2001. Pending the Government's decision on the 
report of Alagh Committee, an interi m reassessment of capacity of 16 high 
capacity urea units has already been carried out w.e.f. 1.4.2000 resulting in a 
saving of Rs. 450 crores per annum approximately. 
Besides, the excess drawal of subs idy on account of non revision of 
consumption norms has also been reported. Keeping in view the 
recommendation of the Joint Parliamentary Committee in 1992, the 
consumption norms were not revised in the VI Pricing Period which was 
extended till 30.6.1997. However, pending Government's decision on the 
policy parameters for the VII and VIII pricing periods including consumption 
norms, the Government has carried out the interim revision of consumption 
norms w.e.f. 1.4.2000 based on the actual levels achieved in 1999-2000, or 
the existing level, whichever is lower. This has led to an estimated recovery 
of Rs. 769 crore per annum.

Stockholm convention 
4701. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SO NI: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has decided to sign the Stockholm convention, a 
landmark Treaty, which focuses on reducing and eliminating release of 12 of 
the most dangerous persistence organic pollutants; 
(b) if so, what would be the purpose of this agreement; 
(c) whether under this agreement the country would achieve total phase 
out of production of Chlorofluorocation and Carbontetrachloride by 2010;

(d) if so how many countries have signed this agreement?

T.R. BAALU): (a) to (d) The Government of India has decided to sign the

Progress in Ganga Action Plan 
4704. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED  KHAN (DURRU): Will the 
Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the progress made so far in implementation of Ganga Action Plan 
and the scheme-wise and phase-wise expenditure thereon; 
(b) how far the implementation is still behind the schedule; and 
(c) the steps being taken to complete the Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) The Ganga Action Plan has been taken up in two phases. 
The Ganga Action Plan Phase I was launched in 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
1985 with the objective of preventing the pollution of river Ganga and to 
improve its water quality. The Plan was completed on 31.03.2000. Against a 
target capacity of 873 million litres per day planned for treatment of waste 
water, a capacity to treat 865 million litres per day has been created. Out of an 
approved cost of Rs. 462.04 crore, an amount of Rs. 451.70 crore has been

and 1996 and is under implementation. Under this Plan, against a target 
capacity of 1860 million litre per day for treatment of waste water a capacity 
to treat 724 million litres per day has been  created so far. Out of the approved 
cost of 1498.86 crore, an amount of about Rs 610 crore has been spent so far.

agencies by way of holding periodic meetings, field visits and monitoring of 
progress of works is done for timely completion of the Plan, by December 
2005.

It provides for a corpus fund to meet the growing requirement of 
opening more creche centers for working and ailing mothers.

Under the scheme financial assistance is given to voluntary 
organisations, local bodies and cooperative institutions engaged in 
the field of women's/social welf are/ women's education. Public

autonomous bodies, and voluntary organisations, to train poor 
women, mostly in non-traditional trades and to ensure their 
employment in these areas. 
5. Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women 
(STEP) 
This Programme seeks to provide updated skills and new 
knowledge to poor and assetless women in the traditional sectors, 
such as, agriculture, animal husbandry, dairying, fisheries, 
handlooms, handicrafts, khadi and village industries, sericulture, 
social forestry and wasteland development for enhancing their 
productivity and income generation.

The scheme seeks to protect and rehabilitate those women and 
girls who are facing social and moral danger due to family 
problems, mental strains, social ostracism, exploitation and other 
causes.

women Self Help-group, Workers. 
8. Condensed Courses of Education & Vocational Training for 
Women (CC&VT)

Board with the objective of providing basic education and skills to 
needy women and also to benefit widows, destitute deserted 
women and also those belonging to economically backward 
classes.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Government is taking adequate steps to improve the 
condition of children in the country. Some examples are: 
1. Under five mortality rate: pet t housand live births, reduced in 5 
years from 109 (1992-93) (NFHS I) to 94.9 (1998-1999) (NFHS 
II). 
2. Infant mortality rate: per thousand live births reduced from 80 
(1990) (SRS) to 68 (1998-1999) (NFHS II). 
3. Underweight prevalence from 53 .4% (1992-93) (NFHS I) to 47% 
(1998-1999) (NFHS II) 
4. Stunting prevalence from 52% (1992-93) (NFHS I) to 45.5% 
(1998-99) (NFHS II). 
5. Wasting prevalence from 17.5% (1992-93) (NFHS I) to 15.5% (1998-
99) (NFHS II). 
180 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6. School attendance, age 6—14 (female) improved from 59% (1992-
93) (NFHS I) to 74% (1998-1999) NFHS II).

93) (NFHS I) to 84% (1998-1999) (NFHS II). 
(d) Several Ministries and Departments of the Government of India are 
implementing various schemes and programmes for the development of 
children. The Reproductive and Child Health Programme was launched in 
1997 providing child health care and maternal services. A major initiative is 
the Sarv Shiksha Abhiyan with the pr imary objective to provide free and 
quality elementary education to all children by 2010. It proposes to cover all 
districts in the country by the end of Ninth Plan. The proposed Constitutional 
(93rd Amendment) Bill, 2001 has the objective of making education of all 
children in the age group of 6—14  years a fundamental right. The 
Government is in the process of finalising a National Nutrition Mission for 
the eradication of malnutrition in the country. The Government proposes to 
adopt a Nation Policy and Charter for Children and establish a National 
Commission for Children to oversee proper implementation of existing laws 
for children and protection of child rights. The Integrated Child Development 
Services Programme delivers an inte grated package of basic services 
including supplementary nutrition, preschool education, immunization, health 
checkup, referral services, nutrition and health education. The programme is 
covering 314.43 lakhs children below 6 years and 62.25 lakh pregnant and

Purchase of sub-standard sleepers from Malaysia 
4760. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the Railways purchased sub-standard sleepers 
worth Rs. 20.3 crore, namely Balau-wooden specials, from Malaysia in 1990, 
from certain supplier, despite the reservations of Forest Research Institute, 
Dehradun; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof, including the names of firms and 
the quantity purchased from each and how much quantity is still lying 
unused with the Railways; and 
(c) what action Government had taken against those firms which 
supplied inferior goods with the connivance of Rail Staff? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) No Sir. In response to a specific reference from 
Ministry of Railways, in Feb. 1986, Forest Research Institute (FRI), 
Dehradun advised that Balau was described as very hard, heavy, strong and 
durable wood and superior to Indian Sal (Shorea Robusta) in all respects; and 
the wood being stronger than Indian Sal wood from strength point of view was 
suitable for Railway sleepers. Later in May, 1987 it also apprised Railways of 
certain inherent drawbacks of Balau wood such as, it was liable to splitting 
on drying and, checking, splitting and surface cracking during air seasoning 
under Malayasian conditions and it recommended procurement of a small 
quantity for trial purpose. As the FRI did not conduct any tests on the Balau 
timber itself and its advice was based on published literature, Indian Railways 
also obtained the first hand information from director, Civil Engineering, 
Ministry of Transport, Malayasian Railways (PKTM) who recommended use 
of Balau wood for Railway sleepers as (PKTM) had been using this wood on 
their system and based on recommendations of FRI and PKTM. Indian 
Railways decided to import a small quantity of 41,399 cum. of Balau wood 
for 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
Railway sleepers. This quantity was considered adequate for conducting field 
trial in varying field conditions on different Zonal Railways. 
In fact, the decision of importing Balau wood was not questionable as 
such, the real problem arose when the supplier did not supply Balau wood and 
instead sleepers made of Kampas wood w e r e  s u p p l i e d .  I n  r e s p e c t  o f  s u p p l y  
made by M/s. Madhya Pradesh. Export Corporation (MPEC), the matter was 
investigated by Railway Board Vigilance and CBI. The concerned Railway 
officials as well as State Government officials have been taken up under DAR 
for the malpractices. On the recomm endation of CBI, proceedings against 
MPEC for banning of business dealings for a period of 5 years have also been 
initiated. Similarly, M/s B.N. Padia's case was investigated, by zonal Railway 
vigilance and they were blacklisted for indulging in malpractices and the 
concerned Railway officials were taken up under DAR. 
(b) A small quantity of sleepers as detailed below has been kept for 
attending to emergencies as further procurement of wooden sleepers was 
banned by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in May 1999 while against item No.3, 
some sleepers have been retained tiU finalisation of CBI investigation.

Technology Mission for Sugar Industry 
4783. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have taken up a Sugar 
Technology Mission for technology upgradation of sugar industry; 
(b) if so, what are the details of  technologies undertaken for 
evaluation; 
(c) what are the findings; and 
(d) to what extent these have been implemented by the sugar industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (d) Technology 
information, Forecasting and Assessment Council (TIFAC) is implementing 
the Mission Mode Project Scheme on Sugar Production Technologies (STM) 
of Department of Science and Technology for improving the technical 
performance of the sugar industry. 
The Mission has prepared modernization schemes for 30 sugar 
factories in the country focusing on  energy conservation, higher plant 
efficiencies, capacity optimization and improvements in sugar quality. The 
Mission has also evaluated 20 new technologies so far. The details of the 
technologies undertaken for evafuation, findings and status of 
implementation are given as under: 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
(i) Thin Film Sulphur Burner for continuous generation of S0 2 gas to 
achieve satisfactory juice clarification parameters. 
Findings: Saving of sulphur, low down time, avoidance of 
pollution, elimination of manual operation, higher clarification 
efficiency. 
Project completed and the technolo gy is replicated in a large 
number of sugar mills. 
(ii) PLC System for clarification Control—PLC based control for Juice 
purification. 
Findings: Stabilized juice flow, automatic control and monitoring 
of clarification process possible, gain in sugar recovery, saving of 
sulphur and lime (i.e. reduction in production cost.) 
Project completed and the technolo gy has been replicated in a 
number of sugar mills. 
(iii) Monitoring and Control System for Pan Boiling—PLC 
based automatic controls for sugar crystallization at vacuum pans. 
Findings: Automatic monitoring and control of sugar 
crystallization leading to low sugar loss in molasses, reduced pan 
boiling time, energy saving. 
Project completed and the technology is under replication. 
(iv) Low Pressure Extraction System (LPE)—a unique system for 
extraction of Juice from prepared sugarcane. 
Findings: Power saving, low maintenance cost, low down time, 
low capital investment at sugarcane juice extraction section. 
Project completed and the technology is ready for replication. 
(v) Syrup Treatment Syst em—for clarification of concentrated juice 
(syrup) prior to crystallization at vacuum pans. 
240 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Findings: Low sugar loss in molasses, better sugar quality and 
reduced processing time. 
Project completed and the technolo gy has been replicated in a 
number of sugar mills. 
(vj) NIR System for determination of sugar content in sugarhouse 
products—a method of quick and reliable assessment of sugar 
content in sugarcane, juice, bagasse and other sugar house 
products. 
Findings': Effective process control, reduces estimation error, 
assists in identifying areas of sugar losses and to reduce them. 
Quality based payment for sugarcane may be possible. 
Project is under implementation at a sugar mill in west U.P. 
(vii) Short Retention Clarifier (SRC) for low retention time of treated 
sugarcane juice during clarification. 
Findings: Use of SRC leads to low inversion of sugar, less colour 
formation* during clarification. The technology is still under trial. 
(viii) Cane Separation System (CSS)—A technology for separation of 
rind and pith of sugarcane before juice extraction to achieve juice 
quality of high order. 
Findings: Extraction of juice through CCS system leads to saving 
of chemicals and produces sugar of superior quality. High revenue 
from sale of rind possible. 
Commercial application of the technology does not appear to be 
feasible. 
(ix) Development of cost and ener gy effective materials for sugar 
industry components—a new zinc Aluminium Alloy developed for 
use as bearings in sugar industry machinery. 
Findings: The new alloy is a cheaper component material with 
comparable or better performance for use in sugar industry. 
The commercial evaluation of the technology has been completed 
and is ready for replication. 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
(x) Masssecuite Filter for separation of crystals from mother liquor 
based on the principle of vacuum filtration. 
Findings: Use of this technology leads to continuous operation, 
energy saving, avoidance of crystal breakage (Uniform product 
size). 
Commercial evaluation of the technology is in progress. 
(xi) Decanter Centrifuge for so lid liquid separation during the 
deliquoring of clarifier underflow. 
Findings: Use of decanter centrifuge for de-liquoring of clarifier 
underflow leads to low sugar losses in the solids, elimination of 
pollution due to bagacilo as no bagacillo is required as filter aid 
and power saving. 
Commercial evaluation is completed and ready for replication. 
(xii) Separate Clarification of Vacuum Filtrates for purification of 
vacuum filtrate separately to eliminate re-circulation of dirty 
filtrates to process. 
Findings: Use of the technology leads to purity rise in vacuum 
filtrate by 1.5 to 2.5 units, treat ed juice is directly added to 
sulphured juice avoiding re-circulation leads to reduced sugar loss 
and better juice quality. 
Commercial evaluation of the technology has been completed and 
the technology has been replicated in number of sugar mills. 
(xiii) Membrane Separation Technology—Pilot scale trials conducted 
successfully through use of po lymeric organic membranes for 
micro/ultra filtration for purification of sugarcane Juice. 
Findings: Achieved a purity rise of 1 to 2 units, may lead to 
enhanced sugar recovery. Observ ed sparklingly clear juice for 
improved sugar quality. Lower consumption of chemicals during 
clarification. 
242 

[10 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(xiv) Entrepreneur Resource Planning (ERP) System— Use of 
IT for efficient plant maintenance and management control. 
Findings: superior decision making for higher profitability. 
The technique is being adopted by a few sugar mills. 
(xv) Raw Melt Sugar Refinery —For production of low colour, 
superior quality international grade sugar. 
Commercial evaluation of the technology has been completed and is 
under replication in two sugar mills. 
(xvi) PTH Device —a system commercially evaluated to minimize 
fouling of evaporator treating su rfaces based on the principle of 
neutralization of free electrons in the calcium ions. 
Findings: Commercial evaluation of the technology has been 
completed and found to be technically/commercially unviable. 
(xvii) Juice Extractor —a new method of extraction of juice using 
principle of displacement of hi gh concentrated juice by low 
concentrated juice. 
Commercial evaluation of the technology is underway. 
(xviii) Automation of Condensing & Cooling System—a PLC 
based automation and control system to create vacuum at pans ancj 
evaporators efficiently. 
Findings: Specific power consumption at condensing and cooling 
station is reduced to between 1.8 to 2.0 KWH per ton of cane 
crushed as against 4.6 KWH per ton of cane crushed 
conventionally. Maintenance of steady vacuum conditions at pans 
and evaporators. 
Commercial evaluation of the technology completed and has been 
replicated in a few sugar mills. 
(xix) Planetary Gear Box—an energy efficient Gear box to transmit the 
drive energy to mill roller for extraction of juice. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2002] 
Findings: Better Power to weight ratio requires less space, higher 
efficiency (approx. 10% more), totally enclosed, less noise and 
vibrations, less oil consumption because of recirculation of oil 
and less maintenance expenses. Co mmercial evaluation has been 
completed and the technology is ready for replication. 
(xx) Chemically Modified Bagasse (CMB) 
The laboratory scale R&D evalua tion work in collaboration with 
Vasant Dada Sugar Institute, Pune has been completed, to explore 
feasibility of converting bagasse into a decolourising agent for 
decolourisation of sugarcane juice, by treatment with Amino based 
reagents. The technology is not viable commercially. 
In the overall, the response of the sugar industry to the in plant 
demonstrations of modernization projects and new technology 
projects through Mission Mode approach, has been very 
encouraging and several multiplier actions are being effected by 
industries themselves based on these results and experiences.

"That this House recommends to the Government that the 
Right to Shelter, 'Right to Employment' and 'Right to Work' 
be included in the Constitution as Fundamental Rights."

RAJYA SABHA            [10 May, 2002] 
Sir, I am moving this Resolution because even after 50 years of 
Independence, we have not been able to provide the basic needs and 
amenities, i.e. shelter, employment and work, to the common people of India. 
Education and drinking water have also not been provided to a large section 
of our society in the country. Therefore, the aim of my bringing this 
Resolution is to give a constitutiona l guarantee to each and every Indian, 
irrespective of caste, creed and colour. Shelter, employment and work should 
be guaranteed as Fundamental Rights. I will first speak about what has been 
happening in the field of. education, and then I will come to shelter. 
Sir, in 1998, the hon. Prime Mi nister, while delivering his speech 
from the Red Fort, had committed that in the next ten years, ten crore 
unemployed people would be provided employment, which meant, one crore 
unemployed would be provided employment every year. Even the 
Rashtrapatiji had committed later in his Address that one crore unemployed 
would be provided employment every year. But this year, they have been 
silent on this subject. What to talk of giving employment to one crore, I don't 
think even ten lakh people have been provided employment by this 
Government. You must also remember that unemployment is increasing at the 
rate of 2.4% annually, whereas the in crease in employment opportunities is a 
mere one per cent.   There is still a gap of 1.4% here. 
Sir, the International Labour Organisation, in its World Employment 
Report, has drawn attention to industrial revival, jobless growth, deteriorating 
quality and decline of employment, elasticity of market-friendly economic 
growth process in the developing countries, including India. This means, that 
the growth of gainful employment is lagging behind the industrial as well as 
the economic growth rate. This was mentioned in the report of the 
International Labour Organisation. Unfortunately, no improvement has taken 
place. Frustration is growing in the country. Your son becomes a graduate; he 
comes out of the college. But he doesn't get a job. He gets frustrated. Today, 
the youth is going on the wrong track. The main reason behind this 
phenomenon is unemployment. How can we solve this problem? The problem 
of unemployment can be tackled by creating more employment. For creating 
more jobs, industrial growth is very importaht. Of course, agricultural growth 
is also equally important for creating work. But what is happening today? 
Almost 90% of our industry is sick today, whether it is the textiles, steel, 
cement, sugar or the chemicals sector. No new industries are coming up.   
You look at the statistics and find out how

industries, and, with the present indust rial sickness, it is impossible to create 
any employment opportunities.   Then, my next point is this. 
Sir, we have to bear in mind that the number of unemployed people 
is rising very sharply. As per estimates, in 1999-2000, there were 9 million 
unemployed people in our country, which would reach 25.94 million in 2007;

Employment and Right to Work be included in the Constitution as 
Fundamental Rights. Sir, I would like to point out that these rights have not 
been conferred on the Indian citizens. Therefore, through this Resolution, we 
want to make these rights as Fundam ental Rights. If these rights had been

the Directive Principles of State Policy have been provided in our 
Constitution, and article 41 states, "The State shall, within the limits of its

the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of
